metadata.title: PISA 2015 RESULTS (VOLUME II): POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR SUCCESSFUL SCHOOLS

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The chapter reports PISA 2015 results using OECD’s PISA 2015 Database and presents associations after accounting for students’ and schools’ socio-economic profile (ESCS). The text does not specify whether student/sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the reported analyses, so the weighting approach cannot be confirmed from the excerpt. For PISA microdata analyses, analysts should use the official PISA student sampling weights and replicate weights (if available in the dataset) to obtain correct standard errors under the complex two-stage sampling design (students nested in schools). The reported figures/tables also indicate that models adjust for ESCS at both student and school levels, which should be implemented consistently with the complex survey design when re-estimating results.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is an OECD PISA 2015 results volume that reports descriptive and association findings (e.g., score differences and correlations) rather than an empirical predictive model with explicitly documented plausible-value (PV) estimation and pooling. The excerpt does not describe a PV estimation strategy or any PV-specific combining rules, so PV handling cannot be verified from the provided text. Missing-data handling is also not documented in the excerpt because the chapter focuses on reporting substantive results and policy interpretations rather than providing a full statistical methods section for PV estimation and missingness treatment.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The excerpt does not provide an analytic-sample construction procedure (e.g., grade restriction, module/task completion filters, or explicit exclusion rules). It reports results from the OECD PISA 2015 Database and indicates that analyses account for ESCS at student and school levels, and that some figures exclude missing values. For re-analysis, use the full available PISA 2015 student sample for the countries/economies included in the reported tables/figures, and apply the same missing-value exclusions as in the original OECD tables (not specified in the excerpt).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD volume reports PISA 2015 results (Volume II) on how school policies and practices relate to students’ science performance and dispositions. The excerpt describes multiple indices constructed from student and principal questionnaires (e.g., perceived teacher feedback, adaptive instruction, enquiry-based instruction, disciplinary climate, truancy, teacher support) and reports score differences and associations after accounting for students’ and schools’ socio-economic profile (ESCS). The chapter also contrasts patterns before vs. after ESCS adjustment and discusses cross-country variation in the prevalence of practices (e.g., frequency of feedback/adaptive teaching, exposure to enquiry-based instruction) and their relationships with science outcomes and epistemic beliefs/career expectations. The excerpt does not provide a full statistical methods section for PV estimation, missing-data treatment, or weighting/replicate design, so re-estimation details cannot be verified from the provided text. Overall, the policy message emphasizes that some teacher-support and adaptive practices are associated with higher science outcomes, while other practices (notably some forms of enquiry-based instruction) show negative associations with science performance, with caution that these are correlational findings rather than causal effects.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is for an OECD PISA 2015 results volume that reports descriptive and association-based findings rather than an empirical machine-learning study with a documented predictive pipeline. As a result, there is no ML target-variable modeling, no reported PV-combining strategy, and no explicit missing-data handling or weighting/replicate design details in the excerpt. The sparse methodological fields (e.g., total_students, per-country n_students, PV handling) reflect that the chapter is structured as a policy results report with references to underlying OECD tables and annexes rather than a self-contained methods paper.
